title: Chapter 51 — The Spirit-Spout
paragraphs: Days, weeks passed, and under easy sail, the ivory Pequod had slowly swept across four separate cruising-grounds: the one off the Azores, the one off the Cape Verdes, the Plate — so called because it lies off the mouth of the Rio de la Plata — and the Carrol Ground, an unmarked watery expanse south of St. Helena.

It was while gliding through these last waters, one serene and moonlit night, when all the waves rolled by like scrolls of silver and, with their soft, spreading seethings, made what seemed a silvery silence rather than a solitude — on such a silent night a silvery jet was seen far ahead of the white bubbles at the bow. Lit up by the moon, it looked celestial; it seemed some plumed and glittering god rising from the sea. Fedallah first sighted this jet. For on these moonlit nights it was his habit to climb to the main masthead and stand lookout there, with the same precision as if it had been day. And yet, though herds of whales were seen by night, not one whaleman in a hundred would venture to lower for them. You can imagine, then, with what feelings the seamen watched this old Oriental perched aloft at such unusual hours, his turban and the moon companions in one sky. But when, after he had spent his regular stint up there for several nights in a row without uttering a single sound — when, after all this silence, his unearthly voice was heard announcing that silvery, moonlit jet, every reclining sailor started to his feet as if some winged spirit had landed in the rigging and hailed the mortal crew. "There she blows!" Had the trumpet of Judgment blown, they could not have quivered more; and yet they felt no terror — rather pleasure. For though it was a most unusual hour, so impressive was the cry, and so deliriously exciting, that almost every soul on board instinctively wanted to lower.

Walking the deck with quick, side-lunging strides, Ahab ordered the topgallant sails and royals set, and every studding-sail spread. The best man in the ship must take the helm. Then, with every masthead manned, the ship, piled high with sail, rolled down before the wind. The strange, upheaving, lifting pull of the breeze from astern, filling the hollows of so many sails, made the buoyant, hovering deck feel like air beneath the feet, while still she rushed along, as if two opposing forces were struggling in her — one to climb straight to heaven, the other to drive, yawing, toward some horizontal goal. And had you watched Ahab's face that night, you would have thought that in him too two different things were at war. While his one live leg made lively echoes along the deck, every stroke of his dead limb sounded like a coffin-tap. On life and death this old man walked. But though the ship sped so swiftly, and though eager glances shot like arrows from every eye, the silvery jet was seen no more that night. Every sailor swore he saw it once, but not a second time.

This midnight spout had almost become a forgotten thing when, some days later — there it was again: at the same silent hour, announced again, spotted by all. But when we set sail to overtake it, it once more vanished as if it had never existed. And so it served us night after night, until no one paid it any attention except to marvel at it. Mysteriously thrown into the clear moonlight or starlight, disappearing again for one, two, or three whole days, and somehow seeming at every new appearance to be advancing still further ahead of us — this solitary jet seemed forever beckoning us on.

Nor, given the ancient superstition of their race and the supernatural aura that seemed in many ways to surround the Pequod, were there lacking some seamen who swore that whenever and wherever it was sighted — at however remote times, or in however far-apart latitudes and longitudes — that unnearable spout was cast by one and the same whale, and that whale was Moby Dick. For a time, there also reigned a sense of peculiar dread at this flitting apparition, as if it were treacherously beckoning us on and on so that the monster might turn around upon us and tear us apart at last in the remotest and most savage seas.

These temporary fears, so vague but so awful, drew a strange power from the contrasting calm of the weather. Beneath all its blue gentleness, some thought there lurked a devilish charm, as for days upon days we voyaged through seas so wearily, so lonesomely mild that all of space, repelled by our vengeful mission, seemed to be emptying itself of life before our funeral-urn prow.

But at last, when we turned eastward, the Cape winds began howling around us, and we rose and fell upon the long, troubled seas that lie there. When the ivory-tusked Pequod bowed sharply to the blast and gored the dark waves in her madness, until showers of silver chips — the foam-flakes — flew over her bulwarks, then all this desolate emptiness of life went away, but gave place to sights more dismal than before.

Close to our bow, strange shapes darted back and forth in the water before us, while thick behind us flew inscrutable sea-ravens. Every morning, perched on our rigging, rows of these birds were seen. Despite our shouting, they stubbornly clung to the ropes for a long time, as though they considered our ship some drifting, uninhabited craft — a thing fated for desolation, and therefore a fitting roosting-place for their homeless selves. And the black sea heaved and heaved, still relentlessly heaving, as if its vast tides were a conscience, and the great soul of the world were in anguish and remorse for the long sin and suffering it had caused.

Cape of Good Hope, do they call you? Rather Cape Tormentoso, as they named you long ago. For, long lured on by the treacherous silences that had attended us before, we found ourselves launched into this tormented sea, where guilty beings transformed into those birds and those fish seemed condemned to swim forever without any harbor in store, or to beat that black air without any horizon. But calm, snow-white, and unchanging — still directing its fountain of feathers toward the sky — still beckoning us on from ahead — the solitary jet would at times appear.

Through all this blackness of the elements, Ahab, though taking almost continual command of the drenched and dangerous deck for the time, showed the gloomiest reserve, and spoke to his mates more seldom than ever. In stormy times like these, after everything above and aloft has been secured, nothing more can be done but wait passively for the outcome of the gale. Then captain and crew become practical fatalists. So, with his ivory leg inserted into its usual hole, and with one hand firmly gripping a shroud, Ahab would stand for hours and hours gazing dead to windward, while an occasional squall of sleet or snow would all but freeze his very eyelashes together. Meanwhile the crew, driven from the forward part of the ship by the dangerous seas that broke bursting over her bows, stood in a line along the bulwarks in the waist; and the better to guard against the leaping waves, each man had slipped himself into a sort of bowline, a loop of rope secured to the rail, in which he swung as in a loosened belt. Few or no words were spoken; and the silent ship, as if manned by painted sailors in wax, tore on day after day through all the swift madness and gladness of the demonic waves. By night the same muteness of humanity before the shrieks of the ocean prevailed; still in silence the men swung in the bowlines; still wordless Ahab stood up to the blast. Even when his worn-out body seemed to be demanding rest, he would not seek that rest in his hammock. Starbuck could never forget the old man's look when, going down into the cabin one night to note how the barometer stood, he saw him sitting bolt upright in his floor-screwed chair with his eyes closed, the rain and half-melted sleet of the storm from which he had come in some time before still slowly dripping from the hat and coat he had not taken off. On the table beside him lay unrolled one of those charts of tides and currents that have been spoken of before. His lantern swung from his tightly clenched hand. Though the body was upright, the head was thrown back so that the closed eyes were pointed toward the needle of the tell-tale that swung from a beam in the ceiling.*
*The cabin-compass is called the tell-tale because without going to the compass at the helm, the Captain, while below, can read the ship's course.
Terrible old man! thought Starbuck with a shudder. Sleeping through this gale, still you steadfastly keep your eye on your purpose.
